Adobe sells software for creating, editing and managing digital content, such as images, video, documents and design. It sells mainly through subscriptions, so customers pay recurring fees to keep using tools that their work depends on.

It makes money from those recurring subscriptions plus enterprise and document services. The business needs little physical capital, which fits with the high ROE in the snapshot. The risk is that new AI tools lower the cost of creating content and give customers alternatives, and I cannot assess that risk from the data provided.

memo.thesis_en: I own General Dynamics, so the question is whether to keep it, and I'm keeping it. It builds nuclear submarines, combat vehicles and Gulfstream jets, and the submarine franchise sits behind a wall of security clearances, specialized shipyards and a single customer that has few alternatives. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 17.2% and debt-to-equity of 0.30, both inside my thresholds, and a margin of safety of 15.1% against an owner-earnings DCF value of about $417 per share. That clears my 15% bar only by a hair, and the DCF leans on an 8% growth cap and a 5% discount rate, so I'm not adding much on that cushion. I bought at $353.20 and the shares are at $354.32, a gain of 0.32% in 28 days. That tells me nothing either way, and I'm not selling a decent franchise because of 28 days. Several checks I would want, such as ten years of earnings, CEO tenure and the history of capital allocation, are not in this snapshot. I can't confirm them from what I was given, so my confidence stays moderate.
memo.thesis_he: אני מחזיק בג'נרל דיינמיקס, ולכן השאלה היא אם להמשיך להחזיק, ואני ממשיך. החברה בונה צוללות גרעיניות, כלי רכב קרביים ומטוסי גאלפסטרים, וזיכיון הצוללות מוגן בחומה של אישורי אבטחה, מספנות מיוחדות ולקוח יחיד שכמעט אין לו חלופות. הנתונים מראים ROE ממוצע של 17.2% לחמש שנים ויחס חוב להון של 0.30, שניהם בתוך הספים שלי, ומרווח ביטחון של 15.1% מול שווי פנימי של כ-417 דולר למניה לפי היוון רווחי בעלים. זה עובר את רף ה-15% בקושי, וההיוון נשען על תקרת צמיחה של 8% וריבית היוון של 5%, ולכן אני לא מוסיף בהרבה על בסיס כרית כזו. קניתי ב-353.20 והמניה ב-354.32, רווח של 0.32% ב-28 ימים. זה לא אומר דבר, ואני לא מוכר זיכיון סביר בגלל 28 ימים. כמה בדיקות שהייתי רוצה, כמו עשר שנות רווחים, כהונת המנכ"ל והיסטוריית הקצאת ההון, חסרות בנתונים. אני לא יכול לאשר אותן ממה שקיבלתי, ולכן הביטחון שלי נשאר בינוני.

memo.moat_analysis: The moat is regulatory and intangible: nuclear submarine construction, with a very small number of qualified shipyards, high security clearances, a captive government customer and multi-decade programs. That position has persisted for decades. The snapshot supports it only indirectly, with a five-year average ROE of 17.2% and debt-to-equity of 0.30. Its weakness is dependence on defense budgets and political risk, plus the Gulfstream jet business, which is more cyclical and competitive. I have no segment data in the snapshot, so I cannot quantify the mix.
memo.two_paragraph_business_description:
General Dynamics designs and builds defense and aerospace products. Its Marine Systems unit builds nuclear-powered submarines and surface ships for the U.S. Navy, Combat Systems makes armored vehicles and munitions, and Technologies provides IT and mission systems to government customers. Most revenue comes from long-term government contracts, with progress payments and cost-plus or fixed-price structures.

The Aerospace segment makes Gulfstream business jets, sold to corporations and wealthy individuals, which adds a more cyclical commercial revenue stream. The company earns money through steady production on multi-year programs, backlog conversion, and service and aftermarket work. Returns come from disciplined execution rather than pricing power in a free market.

memo.thesis_en: We own six shares, bought in August at $216.765, and we are down about 1.93% after 110 days. That is noise, not a thesis change. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 23.8% and debt-to-equity of 0.40, both inside my limits. The owner-earnings DCF gives about $260 a share against a $212.59 price, an 18.2% margin of safety, which clears my 15% bar but not by a mile. The valuation assumes zero growth, so I am not leaning on optimism. I will say plainly that a car dealer's moat is thinner than Coca-Cola's, and I could not verify the ten-year earnings record or CEO tenure from this snapshot. So I keep what we own, I do not add on this evidence, and I keep watching for erosion in the franchise. Price drops alone do not make me sell.
memo.thesis_he: אנחנו מחזיקים שישה מניות, שנקנו באוגוסט ב-216.765 דולר, ואנחנו במינוס של כ-1.93% אחרי 110 ימים. זה רעש, לא שינוי בתזה. הנתונים מראים ROE ממוצע של 23.8% ב-5 שנים ויחס חוב להון של 0.40, שניהם בתוך הגבולות שלי. מודל הרווחי-בעלים נותן כ-260 דולר למניה מול מחיר של 212.59, כלומר מרווח ביטחון של 18.2%, מעל הרף שלי של 15% אבל לא בפער גדול. ההערכה מניחה צמיחה אפסית, כך שאני לא נשען על אופטימיות. אומר ביושר: החפיר של סוחר רכב דק מזה של קוקה-קולה, ומתוך הנתונים שקיבלתי לא יכולתי לאמת עשר שנות רווחיות או את כהונת המנכ"ל. לכן אני ממשיך להחזיק, לא מוסיף על סמך הראיות האלה, ובוחן אם הזכיינות נשחקת. ירידת מחיר לבדה לא תגרום לי למכור.

memo.moat_analysis: The moat is modest. Dealer franchise agreements and state franchise laws protect dealers from manufacturers selling direct, and scale in service and parts gives some staying power. That is a regulatory/intangible moat of limited strength, and it is weaker than a true brand moat. The high ROE of 23.8% (5-year average) is consistent with a franchise, though I cannot confirm from this data that it is durable. The main threats are direct-to-consumer sales, electric vehicles and weaker franchise protection, so I rate durability at about ten years. I do not assume more than that.
memo.two_paragraph_business_description:
Penske Automotive Group is a large automotive retailer. It operates franchised dealerships selling new and used vehicles, and it earns money on each sale, on financing and insurance products, and on service and parts work. The snapshot itself does not describe the business, so I rely on general knowledge here, not on reported figures.

The steadier profit comes from service, parts and finance, which are less cyclical than vehicle sales. The franchise system gives dealers legal protection from the manufacturers, and the company's scale helps with purchasing, brand relationships and acquisitions. The risks are cyclical demand, thin vehicle margins and the possibility that manufacturers change how cars are sold.
